title.en: Gucumatz the Wonderful King: Seven Days of Transformation
title.zh: 奇王庫庫馬茲：七日化形

region.zh: 危地馬拉高地庫馬爾卡赫（烏塔特蘭）（象徵性定位）

texts.period: K'iche' text written c. 1554-78; Ximenez transcription c. 1701-03

source.work: Popol Wuj, Part 4, French ed. Brasseur de Bourbourg, 1861; quoted in Brinton, The Folk-Lore of Yucatan

texts.license: Public domain (Brasseur 1861 French edition); modern translations only paraphrased

summary.en: Truly this Gucumatz became a wonderful king: every seven days he ascended to the sky, and every seven days he followed the path to the abode of the dead; every seven days he put on the nature of a serpent and became truly a serpent; of an eagle, of a tiger, of coagulated blood — and became truly an eagle, a tiger, coagulated blood.
summary.zh: 誠然，這位庫庫馬茲成了奇妙的君王：每七日他昇天，每七日他行至亡者之居；每七日他披蛇性而成真蛇；披鷹性、豹性、凝血之性，而成真鷹、真豹、真凝血。

sensitivity.note: Paraphrase of published translation; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Truly this Gucumatz became a wonderful king. Every seven days he ascended to the sky, and every seven days he followed the path to the abode of the dead; every seven days he put on the nature of a serpent and he became truly a serpent; every seven days he put on the nature of an eagle and again of a tiger, and he became truly an eagle and a tiger; every seven days also he put on the nature of coagulated blood, and then he was nothing else but coagulated blood.
passages.note: Quoted from the Popol Wuj, Part 4, as reproduced in Brinton, The Folk-Lore of Yucatan (Brasseur 1861 base text); not verbatim throughout.

region.zh: 危地馬拉下維拉帕斯拉維納爾

texts.period: K'iche' dance-drama, fifteenth-century (performed to this day); recorded mid-19th c.

source.work: Rabinal Achi, a fifteenth-century Maya dance-drama (K'iche' script; paraphrase after Tedlock 2003)

texts.license: Script is a fifteenth-century K'iche' composition; paraphrase of modern scholarly translations only

summary.en: A K'iche' warrior is captured by the eagle and jaguar knights of Rabinal. Before the king, he refuses to kneel, names his deeds in war, and claims the right to speak before his death. He is feted, fed, and led through the town in the dance of the captive — then sacrificed to the gods of the town, dying on his feet with his own words as his monument.
summary.zh: 一名基切戰士為拉維納爾的鷹與豹騎士所擒。國王面前，他不肯下跪，歷數其戰功，並聲言死前有言語之權。他被設宴款待、餵養，並以俘虜之舞引行全城——終被獻祭於城中諸神，昂然而死，以其言語為碑。

sensitivity.note: Rabinal Achi is a living Maya ceremonial performed annually at Rabinal (January 25, feast of San Pablo); describe respectfully.

passages.text: The K'iche' Achi, captured in war by the warriors of Rabinal, is brought before the lord of the town. He will not kneel: 'I am a K'iche' lord; my heart stands within me.' He names the towns he has fought and the warriors he has faced, and demands that his speech be heard before he dies.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of the Rabinal Achi, scenes of the prisoner's defiance (Tedlock 2003); not verbatim.

passages.text: The lord of Rabinal does not deny him: the prisoner is feted, given cacao and drink and the honored seat, and warned that his death is fixed. 'Then I shall die on my feet,' says the K'iche', 'with my words before me' — and the town prepares the dance of the captive.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of the Rabinal Achi (Tedlock 2003); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: Dennis Tedlock, Rabinal Achi: A Mayan Drama of War and Sacrifice (2003)

narrative.en:
The Rabinal Achi is the one complete pre-Columbian Maya drama to survive, preserved in a K'iche' script from the fifteenth century and performed every January 25 at Rabinal in Baja Verapaz. Its plot is a single action: a K'iche' warrior — the K'iche' Achi — has been captured in war by the eagle and jaguar knights of the town of Rabinal, and the drama is the working out of his death.

Brought before the king, the prisoner refuses to kneel and refuses the honors he is offered until his words are heard. He rehearses his own name and lineage, the battles of the great war between the K'iche' and Rabinal, and the places where he fought. The king of Rabinal answers with something between magnanimity and mockery: he grants the prisoner cacao, drink, a seat, even the companionship of his own daughters' household — but the sentence stands. The prisoner, for his part, asks that his death be honorable: he will die standing, his speech delivered, his name carried by the dance that follows it.

The second half of the drama is the sacrifice in performance. The eagle and jaguar knights — the two military orders of Rabinal — lead the captive through the dance-ground of the town in the dance of the prisoner, amid the sound of drums, trumpets, and whistles, while masked dancers take the parts of the king and his court. The K'iche' Achi is shown the instruments of his death, praises the beauty of his captors' town as a bridegroom praises, and at the climax asks to be tied to the sacrificial scaffold. His heart is given to the gods of Rabinal; the drama ends with the town justified and the prisoner immortal in speech.

As a corpus record, the Rabinal Achi supplies the Maya counterpart of the 'death before honor' cycle in other traditions — the tested hero whose speech is his victory — and preserves a ritual machinery (masked dance, the paired knight orders, the scaffold sacrifice) documented also in the Popol Wuj's ballcourt sacrifices. Its living performance under Catholic feast-day sponsorship makes it a textbook case of a colonial-era survival: the dance continued by being folded into the calendar of the conquering church.

The performance context matters as much as the text. The dance is danced every year on the feast of San Pablo, January 25, in the plaza of Rabinal, with masks, feathers, drums, and the two paired orders of eagle and jaguar knights; the roles are inherited by families, and the drama is taught as a whole, in K'iche', to each new generation of dancers. UNESCO lists it as a Masterpiece of the Intangible Heritage of Humanity precisely because the fifteenth-century script is still the performed script: the prisoner still refuses to kneel, still speaks his lineage, and still dies upright on the scaffold to the sound of the same drums. As a corpus record it anchors the Maya death-and-honor cycle and supplies the closest thing in the Maya corpus to a complete heroic drama.

functions: Charter of the Rabinal annual dance (January 25) still performed with masks and the eagle-jaguar knight pairs
Theology of the honorable captive death: speech, upright posture, sacrifice to town gods
Encodes the K'iche'-Rabinal war cycle as ritual memory

title.en: The Eagle and Jaguar Knights of Rabinal

region.zh: 危地馬拉下維拉帕斯拉維納爾

texts.license: Script is a fifteenth-century K'iche' composition; paraphrase only

summary.en: Two military orders serve the town of Rabinal: the eagle knights and the jaguar knights, masked dancers armed with bows, arrows, and bludgeons. It is they who capture the K'iche' prisoner in the field, they who lead him to the king, and they who execute him at the scaffold — the paired orders frame the entire drama as a single ritual machine of war.
summary.zh: 拉維納爾城有兩支武士團：鷹騎士與豹騎士，戴假面，持弓箭與棍棒。戰場上擒獲基切俘虜者，引其見王者，刑於架下者——皆此二團；一劇之首尾，盡由這對成對的武力圈成。

passages.text: The dance-drama is framed by two military orders of Rabinal, the eagle knights and the jaguar knights, who capture the K'iche' warrior in the field, march him before the king, and conduct the sacrifice at the scaffold — masked, armed with bows and bludgeons, and accompanied by drums, trumpets and whistles.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of the Rabinal Achi (Tedlock 2003); not verbatim.

title.en: The Ball Court in the Sky

region.en: Chichen Itza (Great Ball Court), Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦奇琴伊察大球場

source.work: Stansbury Hagar, The Celestial Bear and the Elements of the Maya and Mexican Zodiacs, in Maya Religion and Mythology collection

summary.en: The second asterism named by the chroniclers is Citlaltlachtli, the Ball Ground: a rectangular figure approximated by the stars of Leo's head, representing the ball courts found in Mexican and Yucatec ruins where the game of tlachtli — Maya, pok-ta-pok — was played. A pictograph in the Borgia Codex shows a deity sacrificed on a court on which the red and black Tezcatlipoca are at play; the ball represents the sun, and the court itself was primarily a temple consecrated by mystic rites.
summary.zh: 編年史所名第二星象即「球場」：一矩形星群，約合獅子座頭部諸星——即墨西哥與猶加敦遺址中所見賽球場之形，特拉斯克利——馬雅語波克塔波克——在此舉行。博爾吉亞抄本繪一神明受祭於球場之上，紅黑特茲卡特利波卡正在對局；球即太陽，而球場本身先是一座經秘儀祝聖的神廟。

passages.text: The second asterism named by Tezozomoc is Citlaltlachtli, Ball ground Asterism. Sahagun shows this as a rectangular figure similar to the ball courts found in various Mexican and Yucatec ruins, in which the favorite game of Tlachtli, Maya Pok-ta-pok, was played. The outlines of the figure are closely approximated by the stars of the head of Leo.
passages.note: Condensed from Stansbury Hagar, Elements of the Maya and Mexican Zodiacs; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: A number of representations of this ball court appear in the codices amongst other astronomical signs. One represents a deity sacrificed on a court upon which the red and black Tezcatlipoca are at play. Brinton and others have shown the probable association of the game with the solar journey, the ball representing the sun; the ball court itself was primarily a temple consecrated by mystic rites.
passages.note: Condensed from Hagar; not verbatim throughout.

title.en: The Ara of Fire Descends at Noon

region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦伊扎馬爾

source.work: Stansbury Hagar, The Elements of the Maya and Mexican Zodiacs, in Maya Religion and Mythology collection

summary.en: At Izamal Cancer is called Kinich Kakmo, the Sun-eye and the Ara of Fire, from the solar rays and a group of stars which were supposed to descend at noon upon an altar, as an ara with fiery plumage descends in its flight. In the codices the ara is often reproduced beside the water goddess. This supposed descent was a feature of the Mayan ritual of the supplementary days under Cancer.
summary.zh: 在伊扎馬爾，巨蟹座名為基尼奇·卡克莫——「日之目」與「火之鸚鵡」——得名於日光，以及相傳正午降於祭壇的星群，正如火羽鸚鵡飛降之姿。抄本中，鸚鵡常繪於水神之側。此「降臨」正是巨蟹座補充日馬雅儀式之一景。

passages.text: At Izamal Cancer is called Kinich Kakmo the Sun-eye and the Ara of Fire, from the solar rays and a group of stars which were supposed to descend at noon upon an altar, as an ara with fiery plumage descends in its flight. In the codices the ara is often reproduced beside the water goddess. This supposed descent was a feature of the Mayan ritual of the supplementary days under Cancer; the Mexican festival in honor of the rain gods and the goddess of salt corresponds in time.
passages.note: Condensed from Stansbury Hagar, Elements of the Maya and Mexican Zodiacs; not verbatim throughout. / Condensed from Hagar; not verbatim throughout.
